---
title: "Reshaping"
subtitle: "≈ `pivot_longer()` · `pivot_wider()` · `separate_*()` · `unite()` · `complete()`"
jupyter: python3
---

Reshaping moves values between positions (column name, row, cell) without
changing them. tidyr and Polars have the same operations under different
names. They differ in what happens when the data doesn't fit: mixed dtypes,
duplicate cells, a wrong number of pieces, and row order. This chapter covers
the verbs, then those cases.

## In tidyverse {#sec-rs-tidyverse}

R4DS's three rules of tidy data: each variable is a column, each observation
is a row, each value is a cell. The tidyr verbs move data into those
positions:

```r
library(tidyr)

who2 |>                                    # lengthen; names hold three variables
  pivot_longer(!(country:year), names_to = c("diagnosis", "gender", "age"),
               names_sep = "_", values_to = "count", values_drop_na = TRUE)

household |>                               # two value columns per child: .value
  pivot_longer(!family, names_to = c(".value", "child"), names_sep = "_",
               values_drop_na = TRUE)

weather |>                                 # widen: one column per origin
  pivot_wider(id_cols = time_hour, names_from = origin, values_from = temp)

penguins |>                                # make implicit missing rows explicit
  count(species, island) |> complete(species, island, fill = list(n = 0))
```

Polars splits the same work across `unpivot()`, `pivot()`, string methods,
`explode()` / `unnest()`, and joins.

## Mental model {#sec-rs-model}

```text
            index         on                          index     variable   value
         ┌─────┬────┐ ┌───────┬───────┐            ┌─────┬────┐ ┌───────┐ ┌───────┐
  WIDE   │ EWR │  1 │ │ 39.02 │ 26.06 │  unpivot   │ EWR │  1 │ │ temp  │ │ 39.02 │   LONG
         │ JFK │  1 │ │ 39.02 │ 26.06 │  ───────►  │ JFK │  1 │ │ temp  │ │ 39.02 │
         └─────┴────┘ └───────┴───────┘            │ EWR │  1 │ │ dewp  │ │ 26.06 │
          origin hour   temp    dewp               │ JFK │  1 │ │ dewp  │ │ 26.06 │
                                                   └─────┴────┘ └───────┘ └───────┘
                       ◄───────  pivot(on="variable", index=["origin", "hour"], values="value")

  unpivot: all `on` columns feed ONE value column        → their dtypes must unify
  pivot  = group_by(index, on).agg(f(values)), then each distinct `on` value
           becomes a column                              → f must give one value per cell
```

Two consequences. `unpivot()` needs a common dtype for the columns it stacks
(@sec-rs-supertype). `pivot()` is an aggregation, so duplicate `(index, on)`
pairs need an aggregate function (@sec-rs-duplicates).

| tidyr argument | Polars argument | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `pivot_longer(cols)` | `unpivot(on=)` | `on=None` = every column not in `index` |
| (implicit: all other columns) | `unpivot(index=)` | **not** implicit: omit it and those columns are dropped |
| `names_to` / `values_to` | `variable_name=` / `value_name=` | defaults `"variable"` / `"value"` |
| `names_sep` / `names_pattern` | `.str.split_exact()` / `.str.extract_groups()` + `unnest()` | a separate step (@sec-rs-names) |
| `values_drop_na = TRUE` | `.drop_nulls("value")` | |
| `id_cols` / `names_from` / `values_from` | `index=` / `on=` / `values=` | |
| `values_fn` | `aggregate_function=` | default: one value per cell, else error |
| `values_fill` | `.fill_null()` afterwards | also fills nulls from the data (@sec-rs-empty-cells) |
| `names_sort = TRUE` | `sort_columns=True` | |
| `names_sep` (wider) | `separator=` | used only with several `values` |

: Argument names {.striped}

One-line translations are in the cheatsheet's
[Reshape](../overview/polars-cheatsheet.qmd#sec-cs-reshape) section.

## Mechanics {#sec-rs-mechanics}

```{python}
#| include: false
%xmode Minimal
```

```{python}
import datetime as dt

import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs
from pl_notes import datasets

penguins_df = datasets.penguins()
weather_df = datasets.weather()

weather_df_jan1 = weather_df.filter(
    pl.col("month") == 1, pl.col("day") == 1, pl.col("hour").is_in([1, 2])
).select("origin", "hour", "temp", "dewp", "humid")
weather_df_jan1
```

### Lengthening: `unpivot()` {#sec-rs-unpivot}

```{python}
weather_df_jan1.unpivot(
    ["temp", "dewp", "humid"], index=["origin", "hour"],
    variable_name="measure", value_name="value",
).sort("origin", "hour", "measure").head(4)
```

`on` takes names or a selector. Without `index`, every column not in `on` is
**dropped**, where `pivot_longer()` would keep it as an identifier:

```{python}
{
    "index given": weather_df_jan1.unpivot(cs.float(), index=["origin", "hour"]).columns,
    "index omitted": weather_df_jan1.unpivot(cs.float()).columns,
}
```

(`melt()`, the old name, no longer exists in 2.0.)

**Row order is unspecified**: the docstring says so, and it changes with the
engine. Eager `unpivot()` stacks column by column; the same query run lazily
came out row by row here, which is `pivot_longer()`'s order:

```{python}
tiny_df = pl.DataFrame({"id": ["a", "b", "c"], "x1": [1, 2, 3], "x2": [4, 5, 6]})

{
    "eager": tiny_df.unpivot(index="id")["id"].to_list(),
    "lazy": tiny_df.lazy().unpivot(index="id").collect()["id"].to_list(),
}
```

On a large lazy frame the rows come in interleaved chunks. If order matters,
`.sort()` by the index and variable columns.

### Names that carry data {#sec-rs-names}

`pivot_longer()` splits names during the pivot. `unpivot()` doesn't; split
the `variable` column afterwards. A small `who2`-style frame:

```{python}
who_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "country": ["Thailand", "Thailand", "Laos"],
    "year": [2012, 2013, 2013],
    "sp_m_014": [120, 98, 15],
    "sp_f_1524": [310, 287, 40],
    "rel_m_65": [None, 12, 3],
})

(
    who_df.unpivot(index=["country", "year"], variable_name="key", value_name="count")
    .with_columns(
        pl.col("key").str.split_exact("_", 2)              # 2 splits → struct of 3 fields
        .struct.rename_fields(["diagnosis", "gender", "age"])
    )
    .unnest("key")                                         # struct fields → columns
    .drop_nulls("count")                                   # values_drop_na = TRUE
    .sort("country", "year", "diagnosis", "gender")
)
```

`split_exact(by, n)` counts **splits**, not pieces, and names the fields
`field_0`, `field_1`, …, hence `rename_fields()`. For `names_pattern`, use
`str.extract_groups()`: named capture groups such as `(?<gender>[mf])` become
the field names, so no rename is needed (see the recipe in @sec-rs-recipes).

```text
 "sp_m_014" ──str.split("_")──────────► ["sp", "m", "014"]     List    any length  → explode()
            ──str.split_exact("_", 2)─► {"sp", "m", "014"}     Struct  fixed fields → unnest()
            ──str.extract_groups(re)──► {diagnosis: "sp", …}   Struct  named fields → unnest()
```

### Several value columns: `.value` {#sec-rs-value}

`.value` in `names_to` means "this part of the name is a column name, not
data". Polars has no sentinel. A `household`-style frame, two columns per
child:

```{python}
household_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "family": [1, 2, 3],
    "dob_child1": [dt.date(1998, 11, 26), dt.date(1996, 6, 22), dt.date(2002, 7, 11)],
    "dob_child2": [dt.date(2000, 1, 29), None, dt.date(2004, 4, 5)],
    "name_child1": ["Malee", "Somchai", "Nok"],
    "name_child2": ["Anan", None, "Ploy"],
})
```

**Route 1: unpivot, split, pivot the `.value` part back out.**

```{python}
(
    household_df.unpivot(index="family")
    .with_columns(pl.col("variable").str.split_exact("_", 1).struct.rename_fields([".value", "child"]))
    .unnest("variable")
    .pivot(".value", index=["family", "child"], values="value")
    .drop_nulls()
    .sort("family", "child")
)
```

It works, but `dob` comes back as `str`: Date and String had to share one
value column on the way (@sec-rs-supertype).

**Route 2: stack the column groups.** One `select()` per child, then
`pl.concat()`. Every column keeps its dtype:

```{python}
pl.concat([
    household_df.select("family", child=pl.lit(c), dob=f"dob_{c}", name=f"name_{c}")
    for c in ["child1", "child2"]
]).drop_nulls().sort("family", "child")
```

### Widening: `pivot()` {#sec-rs-pivot}

```{python}
weather_df_wide = weather_df.pivot("origin", index="time_hour", values="temp")
weather_df_wide.head(3)
```

**Columns** follow the first appearance of each `on` value, like
`pivot_wider()`; `sort_columns=True` sorts them and `on_columns=` picks and
orders them. **Rows** follow the first appearance of each `index` value
(eager `maintain_order=True`). That is not chronological here: `weather` is
sorted by origin, so hours that EWR lacks first appear in the JFK and LGA
blocks and land at the bottom:

```{python}
weather_df_wide["time_hour"].is_sorted(), weather_df_wide.tail(2)
```

With several `values`, names are `{value}{separator}{on}`, as in tidyr:

```{python}
weather_df.pivot("origin", index="time_hour", values=["temp", "dewp"]).columns
```

Non-string `on` values are converted to names (`2007` → `"2007"`, null →
`"null"`). Several `on` columns, e.g. `on=["sex", "year"]`, give
struct-literal names such as `{"male",2007}` instead of tidyr's `male_2007`.
Build one key with `pl.concat_str("sex", "year", separator="_")` and pivot on
that.

### Aggregating cells {#sec-rs-agg}

The mental model said `pivot()` is `group_by().agg()` plus a spread. Proof:

```{python}
pivot_direct = penguins_df.pivot(
    "island", index="species", values="body_mass_g", aggregate_function="mean", sort_columns=True
).sort("species")

pivot_two_step = (
    penguins_df.group_by("species", "island").agg(pl.col("body_mass_g").mean())
    .pivot("island", index="species", values="body_mass_g", sort_columns=True)
    .sort("species")
)
pivot_two_step.equals(pivot_direct)
```

`aggregate_function` takes `"min"`, `"max"`, `"first"`, `"last"`, `"sum"`,
`"mean"`, `"median"`, `"len"`, or an expression on `pl.element()` (the values
in one cell). The default, `None`, means `"item"`: exactly one value per cell,
or a `ComputeError` (@sec-rs-duplicates). tidyr's list-column output is
`implode()`:

```{python}
penguins_df.pivot(
    "island", index="species", values="year",
    aggregate_function=pl.element().unique().sort().implode(), sort_columns=True,
).sort("species")
```

Cells with no rows hold `[]`, the aggregate of nothing (@sec-rs-empty-cells).

### Lazy `pivot()` needs `on_columns=` {#sec-rs-lazy-pivot}

A `LazyFrame` knows its output schema before it reads data
([Data Model](../core/data-model.qmd#sec-dm-containers)). A pivot's schema
depends on the distinct `on` values, so lazy `pivot()` makes you list them:

```{python}
#| error: true
weather_df.lazy().pivot("origin", index="time_hour", values="temp")
```

```{python}
origins = weather_df["origin"].unique().sort()   # the data pass, done eagerly

weather_df.lazy().pivot(
    "origin", on_columns=origins, index="time_hour", values="temp"
).collect_schema()
```

`on_columns` filters as well as lists: an unlisted value is dropped silently,
and a listed value with no data becomes an all-null column.

```{python}
weather_df.lazy().pivot(
    "origin", on_columns=["EWR", "JFK", "BOS"], index="time_hour", values="temp"
).sort("time_hour").collect().head(2)
```

LGA is gone, BOS is empty, nothing warned. Lazy `pivot()` also defaults to
`maintain_order=False`, so its row order changes between runs; sort it.
dbplyr's `pivot_wider()` faces the same problem and runs an extra query to
find the names; Polars makes that step yours.

### Lists and structs: `explode()` and `unnest()` {#sec-rs-nested}

`explode()` ≈ `unnest_longer()`: one row per list element. Null and empty
lists are treated differently:

```{python}
orders_df = pl.DataFrame({"order": [1, 2, 3, 4], "items": [["tea", "milk"], [], None, ["rice"]]})

{
    "default": orders_df.explode("items")["order"].to_list(),
    "keep_nulls=False": orders_df.explode("items", keep_nulls=False)["order"].to_list(),
    "empty_as_null=True": orders_df.explode("items", empty_as_null=True)["order"].to_list(),
}
```

By default the empty order 2 disappears and the null order 3 stays as a null
row. `unnest_longer()`'s default (`keep_empty = FALSE`) drops both, which is
`keep_nulls=False`; `keep_empty = TRUE` keeps both, which is
`empty_as_null=True`. Exploding several columns at once requires equal list
lengths in every row, otherwise `ShapeError`.

`unnest()` ≈ `unnest_wider()`, for **struct** columns. `separator=` prefixes
the field names, like `names_sep`:

```{python}
penguins_df.head(2).select(
    "species", bill=pl.struct(length="bill_length_mm", depth="bill_depth_mm")
).unnest("bill", separator="_")
```

A list column must become a struct first: `.list.to_struct(fields=[...])`
(short lists pad with null), or take elements with
`.list.get(i, null_on_oob=True)`.

### Splitting and uniting strings {#sec-rs-strings}

The three splitters differ in what they return and in how they treat a wrong
number of pieces:

```{python}
codes_df = pl.DataFrame({"key": ["sp_m_014", "ep_m", "sp_f_25_34"]})

codes_df.with_columns(
    split=pl.col("key").str.split("_"),                 # List: all pieces
    split_exact=pl.col("key").str.split_exact("_", 2),  # Struct: exactly 3 fields
    splitn=pl.col("key").str.splitn("_", 3),            # Struct: at most 3, rest in the last
)
```

| tidyr | Polars | Too few pieces | Too many pieces |
|---|---|---|---|
| `separate_longer_delim()` | `str.split()` + `explode()` | n/a | n/a |
| `separate_wider_delim()` | `str.split_exact()` + `unnest()` | null-padded | **dropped** |
| `separate_wider_delim(too_many = "merge")` | `str.splitn()` + `unnest()` | null-padded | kept in the last field |
| `separate_wider_regex()` | `str.extract_groups()` + `unnest()` | no match → all null | no match → all null |

: tidyr errors on a wrong piece count by default; Polars never does {.striped}

`str.split(by, literal=False)` splits on a regex.

`unite()` ≈ `pl.concat_str()`. Non-string columns are cast for you; nulls are
not. `unite()` writes the text `"NA"`; `concat_str()` makes the whole result
null unless `ignore_nulls=True` (≈ `na.rm = TRUE`):

```{python}
parts_df = pl.DataFrame({"diagnosis": ["sp", "rel", None], "gender": ["m", None, "f"], "age": [14, 65, 25]})

parts_df.with_columns(
    key=pl.concat_str("diagnosis", "gender", "age", separator="_"),
    key_skip=pl.concat_str("diagnosis", "gender", "age", separator="_", ignore_nulls=True),
)
```

`unite()` also drops its inputs (`remove = TRUE`); in Polars, `.drop()` them.

### `transpose()` {#sec-rs-transpose}

`t()` for frames. Pass `include_header=True` to keep the old column names, and
`column_names=` to take the new ones from a column. Each new column needs one
dtype, so mixed-type rows come out as `str`; for anything but display,
unpivot + pivot keeps dtypes under control.

```{python}
penguins_df.group_by("species").agg(cs.ends_with("_mm").mean().round(1)).sort("species").transpose(
    include_header=True, header_name="measure", column_names="species"
)
```

### Making implicit missing rows explicit: `complete()` {#sec-rs-complete}

A row that doesn't exist is an *implicit* missing value
([Missing Values](../types/missing.qmd)). `complete()` is a cross join of the
unique values, then a left join of the data onto that grid:

```{python}
penguin_counts_df = penguins_df.group_by("species", "island").agg(n=pl.len())

species_islands_df = penguins_df.select("species").unique().join(
    penguins_df.select("island").unique(), how="cross"              # expand(species, island)
)
(
    species_islands_df
    .join(penguin_counts_df, on=["species", "island"], how="left")  # complete(species, island)
    .with_columns(pl.col("n").fill_null(0))                          # fill = list(n = 0)
    .sort("species", "island")
)
```

| tidyr | Polars |
|---|---|
| `expand(df, a, b)` | `df.select("a").unique().join(df.select("b").unique(), how="cross")` |
| `expand(df, nesting(a, b))` | `df.select("a", "b").unique()` |
| `crossing(a = x, b = y)` | `pl.DataFrame({"a": x}).join(pl.DataFrame({"b": y}), how="cross")` |
| `complete(df, a, b)` | `grid.join(df, on=["a", "b"], how="left")` |
| the missing combinations only | `grid.join(df, on=["a", "b"], how="anti")` |
| `full_seq(x, 1)` in `complete()` | build the grid from `pl.int_range()` / `pl.datetime_range()` |

: `complete()` and friends {.striped}

Join row order is not guaranteed without `maintain_order=`; see
[Joins](joins.qmd).

## Where it bites {#sec-rs-gotchas}

| tidyr behaviour | Polars behaviour |
|---|---|
| `pivot_longer()` keeps non-`cols` columns as ids | `unpivot()` without `index` drops them |
| `pivot_longer()` errors on incompatible types | `unpivot()` casts to a supertype, silently |
| `pivot_longer()` output goes row by row | `unpivot()` row order is unspecified |
| duplicate cells: a warning and list-columns | duplicate cells: `ComputeError` |
| missing combinations are `NA`, whatever `values_fn` is | `"sum"` and `"len"` give 0, the others null |
| `values_fill` fills only missing combinations | `fill_null()` also fills nulls from the data |
| `names_from = c(a, b)` → `a_b` | `on=["a", "b"]` → `{"a","b"}` |
| `separate_wider_*()` errors on a wrong piece count | `split_exact()` pads with null or drops pieces |
| `unite()` writes `"NA"` | `concat_str()` returns null |
| `unnest_longer()` drops `NULL` and empty elements | `explode()` keeps nulls, drops empty lists |

: The differences at a glance {.striped}

### `unpivot()` casts to a supertype {#sec-rs-supertype}

The `value` column has one dtype, so Polars casts every `on` column to their
supertype, without a warning, including casts that destroy meaning:

```{python}
mixed_df = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1], "n": [1], "x": [1.5], "s": ["a"], "d": [dt.date(2013, 1, 1)]})

{
    pair: str(mixed_df.unpivot(list(pair), index="id")["value"].to_list())
    for pair in [("n", "x"), ("n", "s"), ("d", "s"), ("d", "n")]
}
```

Integer + float → float is what R does too. The other three are errors in
`pivot_longer()`, because vctrs won't combine character with double, or Date
with integer. Polars turns the date into `"2013-01-01"` next to a string, and
into `15706` (days since 1970) next to an integer. Only types with no
supertype at all, such as a list and an integer, raise a `SchemaError`.

**Rule:** check the `value` dtype after `unpivot()`. Unpivot same-typed
columns (`on=cs.numeric()`), or use route 2 of @sec-rs-value.

### One cell, two values {#sec-rs-duplicates}

Widen `weather` by origin, keyed by date and hour:

```{python}
#| error: true
weather_df.pivot("origin", index=["month", "day", "hour"], values="temp")
```

`hour` is local clock time. On 3 November 2013 the clocks went back, so 01:00
happened twice. `time_hour` is an instant, so it is unique, and the earlier
pivot worked:

```{python}
weather_df.filter(pl.col("month") == 11, pl.col("day") == 3, pl.col("hour") == 1).select(
    "origin", "hour", "temp", "time_hour"
).sort("origin", "time_hour").head(2)
```

`pivot_wider()` would warn and return list-columns; Polars raises. Find the
duplicates with a grouped count, as R4DS does:

```{python}
weather_df.group_by("origin", "month", "day", "hour").len().filter(pl.col("len") > 1).sort("origin")
```

Then fix the key (`index="time_hour"`) or choose an `aggregate_function`.

### Empty cells are not always null {#sec-rs-empty-cells}

A cell with no rows gets the aggregate of nothing. For `"sum"` and `"len"`
that is 0:

```{python}
{
    agg: penguins_df.pivot("island", index="species", values="year", aggregate_function=agg)
    .filter(pl.col("species") == "Gentoo").select("Dream").item()
    for agg in ["len", "sum", "mean", "first"]
}
```

No Gentoo lives on Dream. A count of 0 is right; a sum of 0 hides the
difference between "measured zero" and "never measured".

The reverse problem: `.fill_null(0)` after a pivot fills missing combinations
*and* nulls that were in the data, because both are null by then.
`values_fill` fills only the former. If the difference matters, pivot a
`"len"` table too and use it to find the real gaps.

### `split_exact()` never complains {#sec-rs-split-silent}

In @sec-rs-strings, `"ep_m"` was padded with null and `"sp_f_25_34"` lost
`"34"`. `separate_wider_delim()` would have stopped. Check the piece count
yourself:

```{python}
codes_df.filter(pl.col("key").str.split("_").list.len() != 3)
```

`extract_groups()` is the same: a non-matching string becomes all nulls.
Anchor the pattern (`^…$`) and filter for the nulls.

### Lists vs structs {#sec-rs-list-struct}

`str.split()` returns a List; `split_exact()`, `splitn()` and
`extract_groups()` return a Struct. `explode()` takes lists and `unnest()`
takes structs, so `str.split()` followed by `unnest()` fails:

```{python}
#| error: true
codes_df.with_columns(pl.col("key").str.split("_")).unnest("key")
```

`explode()` on a plain String column fails the same way: a string is not a
list of characters.

## Recipes {#sec-rs-recipes}

**A summary table, wide by species, for display.** Unpivot, aggregate inside
`pivot()`, and fix the row order with an `Enum` (≈ `fct_inorder()`):

```{python}
measure_cols = ["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm", "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"]

(
    penguins_df.unpivot(measure_cols, index="species", variable_name="measure")
    .with_columns(pl.col("measure").cast(pl.Enum(measure_cols)))
    .pivot("species", index="measure", values="value",
           aggregate_function=pl.element().mean().round(1), sort_columns=True)
    .sort("measure")
)
```

The integer `body_mass_g` was cast to `Float64` to share the `value` column,
which is harmless here.

**Long → wide → long round trip.** Pivoting back recovers the original, once
both sides are sorted:

```{python}
weather_df_measures = weather_df.select("origin", "time_hour", "temp", "dewp", "humid")

weather_df_long = weather_df_measures.unpivot(
    ["temp", "dewp", "humid"], index=["origin", "time_hour"], variable_name="measure"
)
weather_df_back = weather_df_long.pivot("measure", index=["origin", "time_hour"], values="value")

weather_df_back.sort("origin", "time_hour").equals(weather_df_measures.sort("origin", "time_hour"))
```

**Split a sex-and-age code with no separator** (`who`'s `m014`, `f1524`,
`f65`). Optional groups handle the open-ended `65` band:

```{python}
age_codes_df = pl.DataFrame({"code": ["m014", "f1524", "m2534", "f65", "x99"]})

age_codes_df.with_columns(
    pl.col("code").str.extract_groups(r"^(?<sex>[mf])(?<age_lo>0|\d{2})(?<age_hi>\d{2})?$")
).unnest("code").with_columns(cs.starts_with("age").cast(pl.Int8))
```

`x99` doesn't match, so its row is all null.

**Complete an hourly weather grid** (≈ `complete(origin, time_hour =
seq(min, max, by = "hour"))`). Build every hour with `pl.datetime_range()`,
cross it with the origins, and left-join the data. A `True` flag added before
the join marks the rows that existed:

```{python}
hours_df = weather_df.select(
    time_hour=pl.datetime_range(pl.col("time_hour").min(), pl.col("time_hour").max(), "1h")
)
weather_grid_df = weather_df.select(pl.col("origin").unique()).join(hours_df, how="cross")

weather_df_complete = weather_grid_df.join(
    weather_df.with_columns(observed=pl.lit(True)), on=["origin", "time_hour"], how="left"
)
weather_df_complete.group_by("origin").agg(
    added_rows=pl.col("observed").is_null().sum(),
    null_temp=pl.col("temp").is_null().sum(),
).sort("origin")
```

EWR gained 27 rows (implicit missing) and has 28 null temperatures: those 27
plus one null already in the data (explicit missing). The range is
time-zone aware, so 3 November has both 01:00 EDT and 01:00 EST. For a
single time column, `weather_df.sort("origin", "time_hour").upsample(
"time_hour", every="1h", group_by="origin")` builds the same grid in one call
(it needs sorted input; see [Time-Series](../types/timeseries.qmd#sec-ts-resample)).
